objective:
【研究命题·纯机器学习/数学】

解空间刚性 = 满足全部解析约束的函数集合的维数：低维/唯一 = 刚，高维/连续族 = 胖。

核心问题：小型前馈网络的“泛化行为”能否作为 bootstrap 解空间刚性的探针？
令 w = 约束样本数，N_c(w) = 在未参与训练的留出约束点上取得“零违规”所需的最小网络容量（用隐藏层宽度度量）。

【唯一硬性口径（不可更改，其余全由你决定）】
- 零违规 = 留出约束点上的最大绝对误差 ≤ 1e-3。
- 刚性 = 扫描范围内存在较小的有限 N_c（且 N_c 不随 w 增长）；胖 = 扫描上限内任何宽度都达不到零违规（N_c 不可达）。判别是二值的。
- 所有报告数值必须是有限数（禁止 inf/nan/None）。
- 研究对象只能是小型前馈网络本身。严禁把本命题替换或“换名归约”为材料/化学/玻璃/合金/离子导电等任何物理体系，也不要用别的领域类比回答。

【实验的族、样本、扫描、脚本如何设计，以及如何证明“刚性可达”，由你自己决定并给出理由。】

所有结论必须来自真实运行的可复现数值实验：给出扫描设置、训练与留出误差数值、以及 N_c(w) 的数值与趋势。

input_params.description: Design and implement a numerical experiment to test the phase transition hypothesis in the minimal width N_c(w) for zero-violation constraint satisfaction. The experiment will: (1) define a constraint satisfaction problem with w constraints, (2) vary hidden layer width N to find the minimum N_c(w) achieving zero violation (max absolute error ≤ 1e-3 on held-out constraints), (3) scan constraint density ρ = w/H to identify the critical point ρ_c ≈ w/H where N_c(w) transitions from bounded to divergent. Implementation will use small feedforward networks with standard activation functions, and will include convergence checks, validation splits, and repeated trials for statistical robustness. The code will be written in Python with PyTorch, ensuring reproducibility and adherence to the zero-violation criterion.
input_params.expected_prediction: The experiment will reveal a sharp transition in N_c(w) at ρ_c ≈ w/H, where below ρ_c, N_c(w) remains bounded (rigid regime), and above ρ_c, N_c(w) grows rapidly or becomes unattainable (fat regime). The transition will be observed as a discontinuity in the N_c(w) vs. ρ curve, with a clear threshold in the constraint density. The critical density ρ_c will be estimated from the inflection point of the N_c(w) curve.

input_params.description: We will test the hypothesis that zero-violation capacity $N_c(w) = \lceil w / d_{\text{eff}} \rceil$ by designing a numerical experiment on small ReLU networks. We will: (1) generate a family of analytic constraint functions (e.g., polynomials, sinusoids) to serve as target functions; (2) for each target, sweep constraint counts $w \in \{5, 10, 15, \dots, 30\}$ and hidden widths $N \in \{5, 10, \dots, 50\}$; (3) train networks to satisfy constraints with max absolute error $\le 1e-3$ on held-out points; (4) record the minimal $N$ achieving zero violation for each $w$; (5) compute effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}$ via Jacobian rank at constraint points and compare against observed $N_c(w)$. This is a direct test of the algebraic rank hypothesis.
input_params.expected_prediction: For analytic targets, we expect $N_c(w)$ to grow sublinearly with $w$, roughly proportional to $w/d_{\text{eff}}$, with $d_{\text{eff}}$ approximating the rank of the Jacobian of the ReLU feature map at constraint points. If the network is too small, $N_c(w)$ will be undefined (no width achieves zero violation), indicating a "fat" solution space.

input_params.description: We will test the hypothesis that zero-violation capacity $N_c(w)$ exhibits a phase transition at critical constraint density $\rho_c = w/N$ by designing a rigorous numerical experiment on small ReLU networks. Specifically: (1) define the constraint function as a system of linear equations $Wx = b$ (where $W \in \mathbb{R}^{w \times N}$ is the weight matrix and $x \in \mathbb{R}^N$ is the input) to ensure exact zero-violation satisfaction; (2) generate input data samples from a standard normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(0, I_N)$ to compute $\rho$; (3) use a single-layer ReLU network with Xavier initialization to control depth and activation effects; (4) measure basin connectivity via geodesic path finding in weight space between randomly initialized global minima (verified by near-zero loss); and (5) scan width $N \in [10, 100]$ and constraint count $w \in [1, 200]$ with step sizes $\Delta N=5, \Delta w=2$ to identify the transition point where $N_c(w)$ diverges.
input_params.expected_prediction: The experiment will reveal a sharp phase transition at $\rho_c \approx 0.5-0.8$ (typical for ReLU networks), below which all global minima lie in a connected basin (path length < 100 steps in weight space), and above which the landscape fragments into isolated minima clusters (path length > 1000 steps or unreachable), confirming the divergence of $N_c(w)$.

input_params.description: We will test the hypothesis that zero-violation capacity $N_c(w)$ is determined by the algebraic rank of the constraint matrix $A_{ij} = \phi_j(x_i)$ by designing a numerical experiment on small fully-connected ReLU networks. We will: (1) generate constraint points $x_i$ on a 1D interval using an adaptive grid; (2) define basis functions $\phi_j(x)$ as the pre-activation outputs of the first hidden layer; (3) compute the rank of $A$ analytically and numerically; (4) train networks of increasing width $w$ to minimize $\max |f(x_i) - y_i|$; (5) identify the minimum width $N_c(w)$ achieving zero violation ($\le 1e-3$); and (6) verify if rigidity occurs when rank(A) approaches $w$ for $N \ll w$.
input_params.expected_prediction: The minimal width $N_c(w)$ will satisfy $N_c(w) \ge \text{rank}(A)$, and rigidity will manifest as a sharp increase in training error when $\text{rank}(A) \approx w$ for fixed $N$.
